1:
The identity of the king is settled against an old objection. Gill takes him for the Darius the Median who took the kingdom after Belshazzar died, and reports an early critic who made him Darius the Persian, under whom the temple was built, so that Daniel might appear to have lived later than he did; the Ahasuerus named as his father is not the husband of Esther but Astyages. Wesley answers the same objection in the same terms: not the Persian, as some have asserted to invalidate the credibility of the book, but Darius the Mede. Ellicott adds a point from the wording: was made king corresponds with the earlier took the kingdom, and shews Darius was not king in his own right but received his authority from Cyrus. Henry sets the date: he was newly made king of the Chaldeans after Babylon fell, and in this year the seventy years of the captivity ended, though the decree for release had not yet issued.

The books Daniel read are then weighed. Clarke names the two places where the seventy years are foretold and draws an inference from Daniel having them: the people must have been satisfied of that prophet's inspiration, or his prophecies would not have been so speedily collected nor so carefully preserved. Ellicott notes more formally that there existed at this time a collection of sacred books, consisting of what had already been admitted into the canon, and is careful about the reckoning: considerable uncertainty prevailed as to the point from which the seventy years were counted, and three distinct spans can be marked off, from the prophecy to the edict of Cyrus, from one king's captivity to a later reign, and from the destruction of the temple to a later edict. Seventy years had elapsed since Daniel's own captivity, but whether his computation had begun at the right date was to him a question of melancholy importance. Gill and Henry count from the third year or the beginning of the fourth of Jehoiakim, when the desolation began and Daniel himself was carried away, which Henry says he had reason to remember by a good token; Henry adds that the word used here for the desolations is the very word of the older prophecy. Gill fixes the same year as the first of Nebuchadnezzar, through whose reign and his son's and his grandson's the captivity was to run.

What the promise did to its reader is the point Calvin and Henry press. Calvin says the faithful do not so acquiesce in the promises of God as to grow torpid through the certainty of their persuasion, but are rather stimulated to prayer, the true proof of faith being the assurance when we pray that God will perform what he promised; when Daniel understood the deliverance to be at hand, that knowledge made him pray more earnestly than he was accustomed to do. He distinguishes this from the daily habit, from which Daniel had not deviated even when the royal edict forbade prayer and the risk was death; the present prayer is marked extraordinary by the dust and ashes. Faith, he concludes, is no careless speculation, and true confidence in prayer rests on God's word. Henry states the same rule, that God's promises are intended not to supersede but to excite our prayers, and that when we see the day of performance approaching we should the more earnestly plead them; he adds that though Daniel was himself a great prophet he thought it no disparagement to consult another, and that a prime minister to one of the greatest monarchs on earth could still find time to converse with the word of God. Keil and Delitzsch records what became of the prayer in later hands: modern critics have judged it severely, holding its matter and design constructed after older patterns and tracing its clauses to the prayers of Nehemiah and Ezra.
3:
What setting the face means is disputed. Gill takes it of intensity: Daniel set apart time for this service, distinct from his stated hours of prayer and from his civil employment, and turned not only toward Jerusalem as usual but toward the Lord God himself, the phrase denoting fixedness of heart. Ellicott supposes he prayed toward Jerusalem, as on the earlier occasion. Calvin objects that some take the word too fancifully, as though Daniel had looked toward the sanctuary, and renders it that he raised his face toward God: while the altar stood God's face was there, but the temple was now overthrown and neither sanctuary nor ark existed. The earlier turning toward Jerusalem was therefore no desire to pray after the manner of his fathers but an open profession that he dwelt in mind in the land destined for the race of Abraham, a gesture by which the prophet claimed the holy land while still a captive. Clarke supplies the provocation: Daniel found the deliverance could not be far off and yet saw nothing indicating a speedy end of the captivity, and used the kind of prayer prescribed by Solomon at the dedication of the temple.

On the shape of the prayer the voices differ by degrees. Ellicott says it resembles those offered by Ezra and Nehemiah, and that the prayer of Baruch resembles it much more closely. Keil and Delitzsch explains the order: the exile was a well-deserved punishment whose removal could not be hoped for without genuine humiliation under the righteous judgment of God, so Daniel begins by confessing the transgression of the people and the righteousness of God's dealings, that on that ground he might entreat the promised restoration. Calvin states the same as a principle, that the testimony of repentance ought to precede any request for pardon, since God announces he will be easily entreated when men heartily repent; Daniel fills the greater part of his prayer with confession, not for boasting but to instruct us by his example. Gill fixes who is addressed: not idols, nor angels, nor saints departed, but the Lord God of heaven and earth; the confession covers his own sins and his people's, God's justice in afflicting them and his mercy in appointing a time for deliverance.

The two words of the address are then weighed. Both Keil and Delitzsch and Calvin make much of the possessive: if we wish our prayers heard, says the one, the God to whom we pray must become our God; it is by no means superfluous, says the other, since unbelievers flee to God without confidence, disputing whether their prayers will bear fruit. By his confession Daniel shews repentance, by the possessive faith. Calvin adds that Daniel seems to place an obstacle in his own way by opening with the greatness and dreadfulness of God, whose sanctity repels us as soon as we conceive it in the mind. Henry takes the two titles as the two things prayer must hold together. As a God to be feared, he can deal with the most terrible of the church's enemies; as a God to be trusted, he keeps covenant and mercy to those who love him and, as proof of that love, keep his commandments. If we fulfil our part of the bargain he will not fail to fulfil his, and better than his word, for he keeps mercy, something more than was in the covenant; it was proper for Daniel to have his eye on mercy when laying his people's miseries before God, and on the covenant when suing for a promise. Henry adds that every prayer must confess not only sins but our faith and dependence, in the language of our own convictions. Clarke sets fidelity and truth down as characteristics of God, who had never broken his engagements; Ellicott refers the covenant named here to the law given at the mountain.
5:
Four verbs are heaped up, and how they divide is the question. Ellicott reports a scheme of four stages: sin refers to sins of deed, committing iniquity to sins of word, doing wickedly to sins of thought, and rebelling names the person against whom the offence is committed, the result being gathered up in the clause about departing from the precepts. Gill reports another gradation, that some sins were committed through ignorance, some through infirmity and the perverseness of a crooked way, some wilfully and in malice, and some as open hostility, casting off the yoke; he also cites an expositor who divides them into sins of action, word and thought. Keil and Delitzsch works from the words themselves: the first designates sin as an erring from the right, the second as being perverse, the third as passionate rebellion; and he observes that these three had already served Solomon as an exhaustive expression of the consciousness of guilt and had been repeated by the psalmist as the confession of the exiles, so that Daniel adds a fourth term of his own. Calvin declines to divide them and takes the accumulation as rhetoric with a purpose. He allows only that the first word implies not any kind of fault but a serious crime, and that the third is stronger; the copiousness is there because Daniel wished to stimulate himself and the whole people to penitence. We are easily induced to confess ourselves guilty in general, he says, but scarcely one in a hundred is affected with serious remorse; even those who reverently fear God are dull in recounting their sins, acknowledging few and extenuating the magnitude of those they recall.

Calvin also says why the confession is plural: it was the usual method by which Daniel united himself with the people, testifying through all ages the justice of the judgment by which God expelled them from the promised land. He lays down the rule that prayers are not rightly conceived unless founded on faith and repentance, since we cannot please God unless we approach him as criminals resting all our hope on his mercy. Keil and Delitzsch sets the confession against its opposite: God is righteous and faithful, Israel unrighteous and faithless.

The second charge makes the first worse. Ellicott calls it the aggravation of guilt, all the warnings unheeded by high and low alike. Keil and Delitzsch presses the list of hearers: the prophets spoke in God's name to kings and princes, that is the heads of tribes and the great men of the kingdom, and to the fathers, meaning the ancestors, kings and chiefs being separately named; the closing phrase about the whole people of the land means not merely the common people but is added so that no one might be left out. He sets aside the readings that would make the fathers the elders, or merely the teachers. Gill names the prophets who were refused, and says their explanations of the law, their admonitions and counsels were neither believed nor obeyed. Calvin makes the point that this removes the last pretext. They had been instructed in the law and were like a man who stumbles in broad daylight, without excuse and with no one to pity him when he falls; the law was a lamp pointing out the path so clearly that they were wilfully and maliciously blind. He draws two conclusions: that a man who has the law in his hands and turns aside has no defence available, though he use the eloquence of all the rhetoricians and obtain the good opinion of the world; and that there is no rule of holy living except a complete performance of what God commands. He adds that the pairing of commandments with judgments is not idle repetition, as the unskilful suppose, but shews how clear and familiar the instruction was to any who were teachable.
7:
The two halves of the sentence are set against each other. Keil and Delitzsch refuses a rendering that softens it into thine was the righteous cause: the interpolated verb is arbitrary, and the word predicated of God means not a righteous cause but righteousness as a perfection manifested in his dealings toward Israel; the answering phrase means shame that shews in the countenance. Gill takes the first half as essential rather than circumstantial: righteousness is God's nature and appears in all his works, punitive justice belongs to him, and neither the prophet nor any of his countrymen had just reason to complain of the desolations of land and city and temple, since no injustice had been done them. Ellicott says the absolute righteousness of God appears distinct in spite of the chastisement the nation suffers, while the humble looks of its devout part shew that it feels the present shame.

Calvin makes the contrast itself the lesson. God can neither be esteemed just, nor his equity be sufficiently illustrious, unless the mouths of men are closed and all are buried in disgrace and confess themselves subject to just accusation; he cites the apostle's rule that God be justified and every mouth stopped, and glosses it that men must cease to cavil and seek subterfuges. While men are prostrate, God's true glory is illustrated. It follows that we cannot praise God, especially while he chastises us, unless we become ashamed of our sins and feel ourselves destitute of all righteousness; whoever cannot bear this self-condemnation displays a willingness to contend against God, and though hypocrites apparently bear witness to his justice, whenever they claim anything as due to their own worthiness they derogate from their judge at the same moment.

The scattering is then noticed. Clarke observes that the prayer takes in both parts of the nation, the second more widely dispersed and longer in captivity. Ellicott hears in the phrase about all the countries an echo of an older prophecy, and remarks that in the midst of his sorrow the mind of the prophet recurs unconsciously to the great promise of deliverance by the root of Jesse. Calvin draws the opposite point from the same words: those at a distance and those at home were equally subject to God's wrath, and God had not driven all the Jews into Chaldea or Assyria, many remaining among the neighbouring nations, yet Daniel allows them no diminution of guilt though treated more humanely. From this he takes a rule, that the guiltiness of men is not always to be estimated by the amount of their punishment, since God acts very mildly with some who deserve greater severity, whether to allure them to repentance or for reasons unknown; a lighter hand is no ground for self-indulgence.

The repetition in the next verse is deliberate too. Gill takes it as shewing how much the prophet's mind was affected, as fixing the sense in others, and as confessing that he wanted words to express the shame everyone ought to take to himself; it also introduces the list in which every rank is included. Keil and Delitzsch says the thoughts are repeated to set the sin and shame of the people opposite the divine compassion, so that the prayer may pass from confession to supplication for the sin-forgiving grace of the covenant-keeping God. Ellicott makes the same point and adds a grammatical one, that the article implies the absolute mercy of God in the one verse as it implied his absolute righteousness in the other; he quotes Jerome, that after the sentence of the judge the suppliant appeals to his clemency. Calvin observes that naming the kings has a particular force, since kings are accustomed to absolve themselves and their courtiers from all ordinary laws, and that by adding the fathers Daniel comprehends the common people too, so that from first to last all are justly afflicted.
9:
The turn to mercy is the counterweight to the confession. Calvin says Daniel betakes himself to God's mercy as to a sacred asylum, since it is not enough to confess our sins unless we are supported by a confidence of obtaining pardon. Numbers of people, he observes, use great prolixity in bearing witness that they richly deserve every kind of punishment, and no good comes of it, because despair overwhelms them and plunges them into an abyss; recognition of a fault is without profit unless the hope of pardon is added. He grounds that hope on the nature of God rather than on anything in the suppliant, cites the psalmist's saying that there is forgiveness with God that he may be feared, and names two opposite artifices, since Satan either lulls us into torpid security or so agitates us as to absorb our minds in sorrow; we must neither grow torpid in our vices nor be so frightened as to close the gate of pardon against ourselves. Gill fills out the same terms: mercy is God's nature and what he delights in, the fountain of it is with him and many streams flow from it, and the forgiveness of sin is his prerogative and extends to all sins and all sorts of sinners. Clarke states the order of the two words: from God's goodness flow his mercies, and from his mercies his forgivenesses. Keil and Delitzsch takes the verse as the hinge of the prayer, compassion and forgiveness being with the Lord and being what the people need, the thought expanded in the verses that follow.

The particular sin is then named again, and Calvin makes it the aggravating one. Daniel points out one special kind of wickedness, despising the teaching that proceeded from God and was expounded by his prophets; and though no one is excusable by the pretext of ignorance, our wickedness is aggravated when we knowingly reject what God commands. Everything which would have been a fault in the Chaldeans or Assyrians was the most grievous wickedness in the elect people, and their obstinacy was the more provoking because God had pointed out the way and they turned their backs on him. Calvin also reads the word for law here as doctrine in the wide sense, covering not only what came through Moses but the teaching of the prophets, the plural denoting that nothing useful to be known was omitted. Gill puts it more simply, that what was spoken in the law and by the prophets should have been received not as the word of man but as the word of God, so that despising them was despising the Lord.

The extent of the guilt is pressed by Gill: it was God's professing people, on whom he had bestowed distinguishing favours and given a law such as no other people had, and not a few of them or the greater part only but the whole body transgressed it, breaking both tables by idolatry and every manner of impiety.

How the curse comes down is a question about a single verb. Clarke thinks it probable there is an allusion to the punishment of criminals by pouring melted metal upon them, and says this is the proper meaning of the root. Keil and Delitzsch takes the same verb of storms of rain and hail, and especially of the destroying fire-rain of divine wrath, and notes that what is poured out is the curse strengthened by an oath. Ellicott combines the pictures without the executioner: it is poured like a torrent of rain, and as fire melts the silver so the curse causes the nation to melt away. He adds that the threatenings in the law to which Daniel refers had already been noticed by an earlier prophet as partly fulfilled in his own times, so that it remained for Daniel to see the whole pouring out of them.
12:
The argument of these verses is that the event proves the word. Calvin closes every escape: all had come to pass exactly as predicted, so there is no reason to strive with God, whose threats are no vain scarecrows manufactured to frighten children. What use is there in seeking excuses when his truthfulness shines brightly in our own destruction? He adds a sharper form of the point: the word of God would have remained without efficacy had the curse not been suspended over their heads, so that while the people lie prostrate under their calamities the word is borne aloft, and a truthfulness otherwise scarcely perceived is made conspicuous. Gill states the same in a line, that God has made good his threatenings of wrath, and adds that the selfsame things came in the same manner and circumstances as foretold, which he takes as evidence of the truth of divine revelation.

On the judges the voices agree the word is wide. Keil and Delitzsch takes it as comprehending the chiefs of the people, kings and princes together, and Ellicott the same; Keil and Delitzsch also defends the written reading of the word for what God spoke against the margin, which he treats as an explanation inferred from the thought of one definite curse. Wesley presses the office rather than the rank: it was their duty to govern and judge, so a failure was a sin and a judgment both on the people and on the rulers; and the city was a place privileged many ways above all others and punished above all others.

That the punishment failed of its purpose is the next charge. Ellicott says the reference is to the conduct of the nation from the first: there had been plenty of external show of praying, but these prayers were of no effect for their formalism, and the conditions of acceptable prayer are implied in the closing words, a turning from iniquity and a wisdom in the truth. Calvin blames the hardness more severely: fools, as the saying is, require calamities to teach them wisdom, and it was madness to remain stubborn under the rod when the severest blows fell. He draws the rule that the Lord exercises his judgments by not utterly destroying men but holding his final sentence in suspense, to impel them to repentance, having first invited both bad and good gently by his word.

The word rendered watched divides them. Gill says it has the signification of hastening, and reports two Jewish expositors who render it he hath hastened, one observing that the almond tree takes its name from the same root because it blossoms before the other trees; the word so taken denotes God's activity in executing judgment, which does not slumber as some imagine. Calvin sets that reading aside: the phrase implies to him not haste but continual carefulness, the verb being properly used of the guards of cities who keep watch night and day. God uses the metaphor of men far too eager to rush into sin, whose intemperance he answers by declaring that he will be neither slothful nor neglectful in correcting them; though he long endured their wickedness, he was always on the watch and made escape impossible. Clarke takes it of opportunity, that God watched for an occasion to bring these calamities on them, and Wesley of method, the watching denoting the fit ways he takes to punish sinners. Keil and Delitzsch reads it as continual thought, an idea frequent in the older prophet, and takes the next clause as declaring God righteous on the ground of all his works. Ellicott hears in the same word a reference back to that prophet, and reads the verse as the hinge of the petition: as all the curses he foretold have been poured out, so Daniel prays that the release from captivity which he also promised may be accomplished.
15:
The petition rests on an old event. Keil and Delitzsch marks the turn, that after the confession follows the prayer for the turning away of wrath and then for the manifestation of grace, founded on the great fact of the deliverance out of Egypt, by which the Lord made himself a name among the nations. He quotes Jerome, that Daniel is mindful of the ancient benefit in order to call forth a like clemency, but says the remark does not exhaust the thought, since Daniel does not view that deliverance merely as a good deed. Calvin develops that point: when God led his people out he did not set before them a momentary benefit but bore witness to the adoption of the race of Abraham on the condition of being their perpetual Saviour, so that whenever he wishes to gather the dispersed and raise their minds from despair he reminds them that he is their Redeemer. He took them under his care on the very ground of never ceasing to act toward them with the love and anxiety of a father; and when the faithful fear that God has utterly deserted them, they seize on this shield, that he did not lead our fathers out in vain. Gill reads the title itself as an argument, the Lord of the whole earth and the God of this people in a special manner, a description used to encourage faith in prayer. Ellicott traces the language partly to one prophet and partly to another, and notes that the later exile is frequently compared by the second of them to the bondage in Egypt, a thought Daniel reproduces here.

What is asked for according to is then disputed. Gill allows three senses of the word rendered righteousness: punitive justice, since turning wrath from this people would turn it on their enemies; or faithfulness in fulfilling promises, past instances giving encouragement about those not yet accomplished; or goodness, two of the old versions rendering it in all thy mercy. Ellicott takes it of those acts of God which evince his righteousness, that is his faithfulness to his promises. Keil and Delitzsch will not have it softened into a gracious manner, insisting that the word is not grace but the proofs of the divine righteousness, and rejects the reading that makes the sense a hope that as such proofs have hitherto been bound up with a return of grace, so it may be now. Calvin goes the other way with some heat: those who take the word to mean judgment are in error and inexperienced in interpreting the scriptures, since they suppose God's justice opposed to his pity. God's righteousness is manifest especially in the benefits he confers, and the word here stands for his liberality, gratuitous favour, fidelity and protection: he does not fail those who trust him, promises nothing rashly, and is not accustomed to desert those who flee to him, so the plea is for succour by that very justice.

Calvin also notes what the plea leaves out and what it takes in. It excludes whatever merit there might be in the people, who in reality had none, though men always take credit to themselves even when convicted a hundred times over and still desire to conciliate God by pleading some worth of their own; their single hope lay in God having regard to himself alone and by no means to their conduct. And the word all is not idle: Daniel unites so many sins as might drown the people in an abyss a thousand times over, and sets against them the whole sum of God's promised mercies. Ellicott ends on the place named: the holy mountain holds a very important place in prophecy, being the outward visible sign of the stability of God's promises to David, as well as the centre of all that is holy in the kingdom of God.
17:
The closing petitions are read as a lesson in prayer. Calvin says Daniel is wrestling with distrust, and not privately but for the whole church, to whom he sets forth the true method of prayer; doubts break into all our prayers and make our earnestness grow dull and cold, or else we pray without composed confidence and the trembling vitiates whatever we had conceived. Leave off the duty even briefly, he says, and some doubt draws us away and shuts the door of familiar access to God, which is why the sentence is so often repeated. On the next verse he observes that the clause breathes a wonderful fervour, Daniel pouring out his words as if carried out of himself; God's children are often in a kind of ecstasy in prayer, moaning and pleading with much tautology and never satisfied. Hypocrites, he grants, are sometimes superior in mere forms of speech, carried by outward pomps and a heap of words to elegance and splendour; but Daniel displays only a portion of his feelings, wishing to bear witness how fervently he prayed and to inflame others. It would have been enough simply to say hearken; but since God seemed to remain deaf, the prophet begs him to incline his ear, and there is a silent antithesis here, the faithful having seemed to utter words to the deaf while their groans went up for seventy years without the slightest effect.

Why the answer was so long delayed is answered from the same side. Calvin says God's slowness springs from our coldness and dullness, our iniquities interposing an obstacle between ourselves and his ear, and that we foolishly wonder at his not answering as soon as the wish has left our lips. He also notes that Daniel had prayed without any witness and now calls the whole church to witness his zeal, so that the prayer stands as a common form, proceeding not from himself but from God. Clarke says he thinks it scarcely possible for any serious man to read these pleading words without feeling a measure of the prophet's earnestness. Gill takes the petitions in order: the hearing is of the prayers presented and the forgiving of the sins confessed, both to be shewn by removing the present calamities and restoring the former prosperity.

For whose sake the request is made divides the readers sharply. Wesley takes the phrase of the Messiah, to whom the title Lord is often given in the older scriptures, and Gill says the petitions are put up for Christ's sake. Keil and Delitzsch reads the same words as an appeal to God's own honour: the expression is stronger than a simple for thy sake and means because thou art Lord, so that as the Lord in the highest sense God cannot let the desolation of his sanctuary continue without injuring his honour. Ellicott takes the parallel clause the same way and draws a rule from it, that prayer never rises higher than when the soul humbly appeals to God as sovereign lord of all and waits for him to do as he pleases. On the request that God's face would shine, Clarke asks for proof that he is reconciled, and Ellicott glosses it that God's works may shew the fulfilment of his word.

Keil and Delitzsch also presses the form of the last plea. The city is not merely named after God's name, a rendering that enfeebles the expression; the name of God is the revelation of his being, and it is named over Jerusalem in so far as God gloriously revealed himself there, raising the city by choosing it as the place of his throne. Calvin adds the argument the desolation itself supplies: the people had provoked God's anger in many ways and for a long time, yet were oppressed by impious and cruel enemies, so that the severity of the calamity is itself pleaded.
20:
The timing is what every voice fastens on. Gill notes that the prayer was vocal and not mental only, and that the clause is repeated so it might be observed that the answer came while Daniel was on his knees. Ellicott says the same in a line: he had not finished praying when the answer came, and the angel he had seen before comes to reveal the mystery of the seventy weeks. Henry lists the two heads Daniel had insisted on, the confession of his own sin and his people's; Daniel was a very great and good man, he observes, and yet finds sin of his own to confess, for there is not a just man upon earth that does good and sins not, and good men find it an ease to their consciences to complain against themselves. Henry adds what the answer amounts to, the most illustrious prediction of Christ and gospel grace extant in all the older scriptures: if the forerunner was the morning star, this was the day-break to the Sun of righteousness.

Calvin turns the point back on the reader. Daniel's prayers were not useless, since the angel was sent to elevate his mind and lighten his grief, and then to serve the whole church as a minister of grace, inspiring the faithful with hope and encouraging them to bear their afflictions until God opened the way. As for ourselves, he says, we need not wonder at God refusing at times an answer, since those who seem to pray better than the rest scarcely possess a hundredth part of the zeal required; where the difference is so great it is no wonder the success should be so unlike. Clarke draws the other half of the lesson, that God hears such earnest and urgent prayers with delight and sends the speediest answer, the messenger being ordered here to make more than usual speed.

The phrase about the flight is the hardest here. Ellicott calls it a very difficult expression occurring only here, notes that the common English follows two old Greek versions, and reports the defence of that rendering, that the word translated swiftly comes from a root meaning to fly. He allows that the marginal reading with weariness finds supporters, but says that if adopted it must refer to Daniel's own bodily condition after the earlier vision, and that the first translation suits the context best; the flight of angels, he adds, is implied in an older prophet. Calvin reports the same two derivations without deciding, one from the verb to fly and the other from a verb meaning to grow weary. Ellicott observes that touched is literally reached, and Clarke and Calvin note that the messenger is called a man because he appeared in that form.

The hour named raises a question of its own, there being no altar. Calvin faces it directly: seventy years had passed in which Daniel never saw a sacrifice offered, and yet he still reckons by the evening sacrifice as though he attended daily in a temple that did not exist. He concludes that God's servants, though deprived of the outward means of grace, can still make them useful by meditating on the rites of God's institution; a man imprisoned and forbidden the Lord's Supper to the end of his life ought not to throw away the remembrance of that sacred symbol, but should consider daily why it was given. Wesley says the same of the people: the hour was a solemn and set time of devotion, and though the altar was in ruins the pious were daily thoughtful of when the offering should have been made, hoping their prayer would be set forth as incense and the lifting of their hands as the evening sacrifice; the offering was a type of the great sacrifice, in virtue of which Daniel's prayer was accepted when he prayed for the Lord's sake.
22:
Ellicott states what the difficulty was. The word means that the angel gave Daniel understanding, and the understanding was in the perplexing words of the older prophet, shewing him that what concerned his people was a period of seventy weeks still to come rather than the seventy years already passed. Gill takes the same verb two ways: either that the angel informed him by talking of the will of God, to restore the captivity of his people, to rebuild Jerusalem and the temple, and of the coming of the Messiah; or that he caused him to attend, making him advert to the discourse in order to understand it. Keil and Delitzsch simply marks the weight of what follows, that this message of the angel relates to the most important revelations concerning the future development of the kingdom of God.

Calvin turns the angel's errand into an obligation on the hearer. Daniel ought to learn from the angel's duty what he himself ought to do; God had honoured him so highly as to set one of his angels before him as master and teacher, and the prophet ought not to neglect so singular a favour lest he seem ungrateful. We ought to reflect on the same whenever we enter God's temple or read any passage of holy scripture, and acknowledge that teachers are sent from God to assist our ignorance and interpret the scriptures for us; scripture is given that we may find there what would otherwise be hidden, God opening his own heart when he makes known his secrets by the law and the prophets and the apostles. He cites the apostle's phrase that the gospel is preached for the obedience of faith, and glosses it that we shall not escape with impunity unless we embrace that doctrine, since otherwise we do our utmost to frustrate the designs of God.

On the next verse Calvin says the angel not only exacts docility but exhorts to greater attention than usual, since this singular and extraordinary prophecy needed no common study. He declines to recite the opinions of others on the clause about the commandment going forth, and takes the genuine sense to be that God heard the prayers of his servant and then promulgated what he had already decreed; the verb expresses the publication of a decree formerly made, as the decrees of princes go forth when publicly spread abroad. God had determined what he would do the moment Daniel ceased, for his counsel never fails; and the point of saying so is the impossibility of the prayers of his saints being in vain, since he grants them the very thing he would have bestowed had they not prayed for it, as though obedient to their desires. It is clear enough, he adds, that we can obtain nothing by prayer without God's previous determination to grant it, yet the two are not contrary, since he both performs the wishes of those who fear him and executes what he determined before the creation of the world.

Gill draws the same lesson from the timing, that the answer came as soon as Daniel began to pray, which shews how ready the Lord is to hear; yet it was not owing to the prophet's prayers, nor to any intrinsic virtue or merit in them, that what follows was done, and besides, more is revealed and promised than Daniel had asked for. Ellicott prefers the marginal rendering of the same clause, which points forward to the revelation that follows rather than back to anything already given. On the title used of the prophet he notes that it occurs again in the next chapter and implies that Daniel was worthy of this proof of God's love, and reports Jerome comparing the name Jedidiah given to another man for a like reason.
24:
What kind of weeks these are must be settled first. Ellicott says great difficulty attends the question: the verses that follow shew that ordinary weeks cannot be meant, yet it is remarkable that in the law the word week is never used for a period of seven years. It is generally assumed they consist of years, on the principle of passages where a day stands for a year. Gill argues from the content, that weeks of days are far too short for so many events, so weeks of years are meant and the number is four hundred and ninety; Wesley says the same. Calvin supplies a reason nobody on his own side has offered: years are reckoned by weeks in order to set seventy weeks of years against the seventy years of the older prophecy, so grace is measured against judgment. The people had been punished by an exile of seventy years, and a period of favour of sevenfold duration now follows, shining with continual splendour, shaded with a few clouds.

The verb rendered determined is also disputed. Ellicott observes that it occurs only here and that the old versions render it three ways; in a cognate tongue it means to cut, and so to determine, and what is determined is twofold, sin on one hand and righteousness on the other. Calvin reports a reading that takes it as cut off, marking the continual miseries of the people, and answers that taken to mean terminate the angel announces the conclusion of the weeks.

The six clauses are then weighed. Ellicott notes that the margin offers to restrain in place of to finish, meaning to hold sin back from spreading, parallel with the other marginal alternative, to seal up; but he judges these more probably conjectures of early critics, since the word for sealing already stands in the last clause. On the sealing of vision he reports that the translators supposed all visions were to be fulfilled within the seventy weeks, and holds it more agreeable to the context that the prophet speaks of the absolute cessation of all prophecy. Wesley divides the six into three that name the disease and three the cure, and takes the everlasting righteousness, a phrase Ellicott notes occurs nowhere else, as justification by free grace, everlasting because Christ is eternal.

The last clause turns on two words. Ellicott lists some fifteen things the phrase most Holy is used of in scripture, from the altar and the atonement to the shewbread and the sanctuary of a later vision, and says only the context decides. From the way the next verse is joined on by the words know therefore, he concludes that the phrase stands parallel to Messiah the Prince and indicates a person; so one old translator, who renders it Messiah the most Holy, and a Greek version whose verb would have no meaning if applied to a place. Wesley reads the anointing as an allusion to the name Messiah, which signifies anointed, and distributes it over the conception, the baptism and the three offices.

Where the reckoning starts is left open. Clarke says the chief difficulty is to find the time from which the weeks should be dated, and observes that the angel's words are not a direct answer to the prayer: Daniel asked when the seventy years of the captivity would end, and was shewn seventy weeks determined about a redemption from another sort of captivity, beginning with the edict to rebuild Jerusalem and ending with the death of Messiah the Prince and the abolition of the sacrifices. Calvin rejects the reckoning that begins at the destruction of the first temple and closes at the overthrow of the second, since it heaps together six hundred years; the seventy years must close before the reign of Cyrus, the record stating that when they were complete God stirred up his spirit to free the people.
25:
Where the sentence divides is a textual question. Ellicott says the difficulty is much increased by the principal accent standing after the words seven weeks, since on that punctuation the sense is that unto an anointed prince shall be seven weeks, and during sixty and two weeks the city shall be built. He rejects it as against the ancient translations, with one exception, and against the next verse, which ties the sixty-two weeks to the Anointed, not to the building. Keil and Delitzsch takes the opposite view of the same accents, holding the two parts rightly separated by the Masoretes, and adds that know therefore and understand announces no new prophecy but points to the importance of what is now opened, these three verses explicating the one before. Gill reads the opening as a call to observe the beginning of the weeks and what should be accomplished in them. Calvin defends the order of the numbers against the objection that Hebrew habitually puts the smaller first. He confesses the idiom, but says the prophet is not relating one continuous series; he marks off seven weeks and then cuts away sixty-two, so the seven precede in time.

Which decree is meant is not agreed. Ellicott takes the word for commandment, as in the verse before, of a revelation, and asks whether the allusion is to the edict of Cyrus, predicted by an older prophet, or to what happened in the twentieth year of a later king; there is no reference to the earlier prophecy about the seventy years, since nothing there reads as a command to rebuild Jerusalem. Wesley leaves it open between two kings. Clarke fixes it by counting backwards: from the death of Christ at the passover in a stated year of the Julian period, four hundred and ninety years lead back to the month of Ezra's commission from Artaxerxes Longimanus. The whole divides into forty-nine years for restoring the city, four hundred and thirty-four to the public entrance of the Messiah on his ministry, and a last seven taking in the ministry of John the Baptist with our Lord's. Calvin fixes no year but a condition, that the angel speaks of the edict about bringing back the people and restoring the city, so it is foolish to apply the words to a time when the city was not restored and no decree published.

Who the anointed prince is divides them again. Calvin reports that some take the singular noun as a plural meaning the priests, others referring it to the governor who led the return and others to the high priest of that day; he holds the angel speaks of Christ, of whom kings and priests under the law were a type. He answers those who think the dignity of Christ lessened by the word rendered prince or leader, as though such leadership had neither sceptre nor diadem: David is called a leader of the people, and so is a later king wearing his diadem; the word implies superior excellence. Ellicott reads the phrase literally as an anointed one, a prince, two nouns in apposition with the article omitted because person and office are definite without it, and the anointing making him king and priest at once; the foreign king elsewhere called an anointed of the Lord cannot be meant, since by no calculation did he come seven or sixty-nine weeks from the start of the captivity.

The last clauses get less confident treatment. Ellicott takes the street for the large square in front of the temple, and says the contrasted word rendered wall cannot be made out, though by etymology it means something cut off. The troublous times he reads out of the history itself, one long tale of opposition from the persecution the returning governor endured to the destruction of what had been built, the walls not finished until the twentieth year of a later king.
26:
Where in the count the cutting off falls is settled first. Ellicott says the words can only mean that in the seventieth week the Anointed is cut off, and points to the care with which the whole is arranged as seven weeks, then sixty-two, then one; the city is rebuilt during the first seven, though the troublous times may extend over the sixty-two. Keil and Delitzsch qualifies it: from the word after it does not certainly follow that the cutting off falls wholly at the beginning of the seventieth week, only that it is the first great event of that week. On the verb he says it means to hew down or fell, and so to be rooted up, denoting generally a violent death, an uprooting from among the living or from the congregation. Gill and Wesley simply add the numbers, the sixty-two reckoned from the end of the first seven, which together make four hundred and eighty-three years.

Who is cut off comes next. Ellicott says the Messiah here must be the same person spoken of before, and notes that the Greek versions read unction rather than anointed, so that one early writer explained the cutting off as the cessation of the unction by which sovereignty was established; but the verb applies more appropriately to a person than a thing, is frequently used of excommunication, and must not be confused with a different verb rendered the same way elsewhere. Calvin takes the clause as a prediction of the death of Christ and rejects three rival identifications, one with a king of the following century, one with an earlier high priest, and the extension of the words to the priesthood at large, which he calls forced and absurd.

The words rendered but not for himself are frankly obscure. Ellicott says they mean literally only and he has not, what he loses being left indefinite; taking the sense from the context, the meaning is either that he has no more a people or that his office of Messiah among them ceases. Calvin surveys the same possibilities and rejects them all as too frigid: that the city or people shall be as nothing to him; that his death shall be neither hostile nor favourable; that nothing shall remain to him, in the sense of being destitute of all help. His own reading is that Christ should so die as to be entirely reduced to nothing. Wesley reads the clause differently again, not of loss but of purpose, that he was cut off not for himself but for our sakes and our salvation.

The destroyer is named without hesitation by some and with much by others. Clarke says that by the prince Titus, the son of Vespasian, is plainly intended, and the people of that prince are the Romans, who destroyed the holy place and swept all away as a flood until the war was finished; Wesley names the same people and commander, and takes the closing word to mean that God had decreed to destroy that place and people by the miseries of war. Ellicott is more cautious. The word prince, applied to the Messiah in the verse before, is here used of another person, some secular prince set in opposition to him, and the phrase that shall come implies hostile intent. Two such princes have already appeared in the book, Antiochus and his great antitype Antichrist, but this appears to be neither; a further typical prince is introduced who shall destroy city and sanctuary after the rejection of the Messiah, and the work of destruction is attributed to the people and not to the prince at all. On the phrase about the end he says it is not clear what end or whose end is meant, since by the rules of grammar the possessive may refer either to the sanctuary, the last substantive, or to the prince, the chief nominative.
27:
Who confirms the covenant is left open. Keil and Delitzsch reports that many, following one Greek version, make one week the subject, so that one week shall confirm the covenant to many; he rejects it, since that mode is admissible only where the subject comes after the action, whereas confirming a covenant is the deed of a person, not the work of time, and since the notes of time here connect with those before. Ellicott lists more: another Greek version makes the covenant itself the subject, others the Antichristian prince of the last verse, on which reading the covenant is the agreement he makes with the many who apostatise. He answers that the word covenant applies not to such an agreement but to a covenant with God, and that in the previous verse it is the people of the prince and not the prince who are the subject; so it is better to take the Messiah, and to read that in the last week, though cut off, he confirms God's covenant with those who receive him. Wesley takes it the same way and lists the means, the testimony of witnesses, the preaching, the signs, the holy life and the death. Calvin also reads it of Christ, tying the clause to the earlier title of Leader: Christ assumed the kingly office when he promulgated the grace of God, and that is the confirmation meant. The covenant under the law was sure in itself but weak as far as man was concerned, whereas this one holds because we have been reconciled by the death of Christ, the law inscribed not on stones but on hearts of flesh. Gill alone dissents on chronological ground: the covenant of grace is not confirmed for one week but for ever; he refers the clause to the Roman people named at the close of the previous verse, who made peace with many nations, the Medes, Parthians and Armenians among them, for seven years, to accomplish their design against the city.

On the ceasing of the sacrifice there is less distance. Ellicott renders the phrase in the midst of the week or during half of it, the latter half according to one Greek version, and takes what ceases to be all the Mosaic sacrifices. Wesley says the same of the Jewish rites and the Levitical worship, ended for ever by the death of Christ.

The clause about the abomination is the hardest here, and the two who face it disagree about the text. Clarke calls it remarkably obscure: the literal rendering is upon the wing of abominations causing amazement, and yields no determinate sense. He reports a Hebrew manuscript of the thirteenth century preserving a remarkable reading, that in the temple there shall be abomination, and says it frees the place from all embarrassment and agrees with the words quoted in the gospel about the abomination standing in the holy place. Ellicott agrees that the Greek versions and Jerome give that sense, but says no such meaning can be got from the Hebrew text without omitting the last letter and altering the last vowel of the word translated abominations. As it stands the text renders only as upon the wing of abominations is a desolator, the person who causes the desolations already mentioned. What the wing of abominations means he leaves unsettled: the language is without parallel except in psalms that use the plural, and if the number is disregarded the sense is that idolatry is the power by which the desolator works, riding on those wings as God rides on the winds; but he thinks it decisive that the prophet wrote wing, not wings. Keil and Delitzsch notes that the verse contains four statements. On the last, Wesley takes what is determined to be the spirit of slumber God has decreed to pour on the desolate nation until the time when all Israel shall be saved.
